```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(sta310r)
```

This vignette presents `dataset_by_exercise`, the index that links every data
set in `sta310r` to the worked examples in Collett (2023) that use it. The same
index is available as a data set, so you can filter and sort it in R rather than
reading it here.

## The `dX.Y` aliases

Each example that uses a data set gives that data set an alias `dX.Y`, where
`X.Y` is the number of the example. For example, Example 3.7 uses the
`myeloma` data, so `d3.7` is an alias for `myeloma`:

```{r}
identical(d3.7, myeloma)
dim(d3.7)
```

A data set that is used in more than one example has one alias per example.
The aliases are ordinary data objects in the package, so `d3.7` works after
`library(sta310r)` just like `myeloma` does, and `?d3.7` opens the help page of
the data set. The index below is the authoritative list of which alias belongs
to which example.

## Index by data set

One row per data set, with its aliases and example numbers collapsed into a
single string. The full index, with one row per data set and example, is in the
next section.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
index <- dataset_by_exercise

by_dataset <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(index, index$dataset), function(x) {
  used <- x[!is.na(x$alias), , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(
    data_set = x$dataset[1],
    title = x$dataset_title[1],
    aliases = if (nrow(used)) paste(used$alias, collapse = ", ") else "—",
    examples = if (nrow(used)) paste(used$example, collapse = ", ") else "—",
    rows = x$n_rows[1],
    variables = x$n_variables[1],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
by_dataset <- by_dataset[order(by_dataset$data_set), ]
rownames(by_dataset) <- NULL

knitr::kable(
  by_dataset,
  col.names = c("Data set", "Title", "Aliases", "Examples", "Rows", "Variables")
)
```

## Index by example

The full index, ordered by chapter and example. Rows without an alias are data
sets that are not used in a numbered example; the `note` column says where they
come from.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
full <- dataset_by_exercise
full$note[is.na(full$note)] <- ""
knitr::kable(
  full[, c("example", "alias", "dataset", "example_title", "note")],
  col.names = c("Example", "Alias", "Data set", "Example title", "Note")
)
```

## Data sets without a numbered example

Four of the data sets from the book are used in the appendices rather than in a
numbered example, and the Scottish cohort is course material rather than book
data. They have no `dX.Y` alias:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
no_alias <- index[is.na(index$alias), c("dataset", "dataset_title", "note")]
knitr::kable(
  no_alias,
  col.names = c("Data set", "Title", "Note")
)
```

The cirrhosis study is a special case. Example 8.4 uses three forms of the same
data: `cirrhosis` (the baseline values, alias `d8.4`), `cirrhosis_lbr` (the
log-bilirubin measurements in long format) and `cirrhosis_cp` (the counting
process format). Only the baseline object has the alias; the other two are
listed with the same example but without an alias.

## Using the index in R

Because the index is a data frame, you can query it directly:

```{r}
# Which data set does Example 8.3 use?
dataset_by_exercise$dataset[dataset_by_exercise$example == "8.3"]

# Which examples use the myeloma data?
subset(dataset_by_exercise, dataset == "myeloma", c("alias", "example"))

# All data sets used in Chapter 3
unique(dataset_by_exercise$dataset[dataset_by_exercise$chapter == 3])
```

The index is generated by `data-raw/dataset_by_exercise.R`. If a new data set
is added, or the example mapping changes, update that script and re-run it; it
recreates both `dataset_by_exercise` and the `dX.Y` aliases.

## Reproducing the book's analyses

The help page of every data set shows how the analyses in Collett (2023) are
carried out in R, with a comment for each example number. Each page has two
parts:

* **Collett (2023), Chapter 17 style** uses the functions and packages of the
  book's own R chapter: `survival::survfit()`, `survival::coxph()`,
  `survival::survdiff()`, `survival::survreg()`, `survival::cox.zph()`,
  `survival::tmerge()`, `survival::survSplit()`, `penalized::penalized()`,
  `eha::pchreg()` and `cmprsk::cuminc()` / `cmprsk::crr()`.
* **Modern tools** repeats the same analysis with newer packages:
  `ggsurvfit`, `flexsurv`, `coxme`, `icenReg`, `tidycmprsk`, `broom`, `rms`
  and `glmnet`.

For example, `?gastric` shows the piecewise treatment effect of Examples 11.2
and 11.3, and `?iud` shows the conjugate Bayesian analysis of Examples 16.1 to
16.3 alongside the parametric models of Examples 5.1 to 5.4. Where the book
uses a package that is not a dependency of this package, the help page says so
in a comment and uses a runnable equivalent.
